⚠ Why this isn't obvious — what the wire argument does not prove

"Magnetism is just relativity applied to electrostatics" is a true and beautiful slogan and it is routinely overstated. Precisely what was used above:

  1. Coulomb's law, for the field of a static line charge. Input.
  2. Charge invariance. Without it, λ+′=γuλ0\lambda'_{+}=\gamma_{u}\lambda_{0}λ+′​=γu​λ0​ is false and the whole calculation collapses. This is an experimental fact — the ⚑ callout at the head of the chapter — not a consequence of relativity.
  3. The field concept — that the force is mediated by something local, so that "the field at the test charge" is a meaningful quantity to transform. A pure action-at-a-distance theory would need a different argument.
  4. The Lorentz force law in the lab, to have something to compare against.

What relativity supplies is the relation between the two descriptions, and it supplies it with no freedom at all. Given Coulomb, charge invariance and the field concept, the magnetic force is not optional and its magnitude is fixed. That is a very strong statement — it means the constant μ0\mu_{0}μ0​ is not independent of ϵ0\epsilon_{0}ϵ0​, which is Chapter 2.1's c=1/μ0ϵ0c=1/\sqrt{\mu_{0}\epsilon_{0}}c=1/μ0​ϵ0​​ arriving from the other direction. But it is not the same as "magnetism can be derived from electrostatics alone", which is false.

In plain terms 2.6.6

The argument making the claim literal is checkable against a current balance. A current-carrying wire is electrically neutral in the laboratory, which is experiment and not assumption, since a live wire does not attract a pith ball, so a charge moving alongside feels a purely magnetic force. Now board that charge. In its own frame nothing moves, so no magnetic force is available, yet it still accelerates towards the wire, whether it strikes not being a matter of opinion.

Something else is doing the work, and there is one candidate. The wire holds two populations of charge, a lattice at rest and a gas of electrons drifting through it, contracting by different factors when frames change, the electrons having been moving already and the lattice not. The cancellation that made the wire neutral is spoiled, the wire carries a net charge, and the attraction is ordinary electrostatics. Both compute the same trajectory and neither description is deeper.

The numbers make it startling. Electrons drift along a copper wire at under a tenth of a millimetre per second, two and a half parts in ten million million of light speed, so magnetism is an effect of that size. Electromagnets lift cars because the unbalanced quantity is colossal: thirteen thousand coulombs of mobile charge per metre, cancelled to that precision by the lattice. A minute fractional imbalance in an enormous cancellation is still a substantial charge.

7 · The invariants

If E\vv EE and B\vv BB separately are observer-dependent, what do all observers agree about? By Chapter 2.4 §5.1 the answer is: whatever you can build by contracting every index. From a single antisymmetric rank-2 tensor there are exactly two such quantities.

7.1 · The first invariant

Contract FFF with itself:

FμνFμν  =  ∑μ,νFμνFμν. F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} \;=\; \sum_{\mu,\nu}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}. Fμν​Fμν=μ,ν∑​Fμν​Fμν. (2.6.53)

Split the double sum by index type. The diagonal contributes nothing. The 0i0i0i and i0i0i0 entries contribute twice over (once each way), and by (2.6.17) F0iF0i=(Ei/c)(−Ei/c)=−(Ei)2/c2F_{0i}F^{0i}=(E^{i}/c)(-E^{i}/c)=-(E^{i})^{2}/c^{2}F0i​F0i=(Ei/c)(−Ei/c)=−(Ei)2/c2, so those terms give

2∑iF0iF0i  =  −2c2(Ex2+Ey2+Ez2)  =  −2E2c2. 2\sum_{i}F_{0i}F^{0i} \;=\; -\frac{2}{c^{2}}\big(E_{x}^{2}+E_{y}^{2}+E_{z}^{2}\big) \;=\; -\frac{2E^{2}}{c^{2}}. 2i∑​F0i​F0i=−c22​(Ex2​+Ey2​+Ez2​)=−c22E2​. (2.6.54)

For the purely spatial entries, Fij=Fij=−ϵijkBkF_{ij}=F^{ij}=-\epsilon^{ijk}B^{k}Fij​=Fij=−ϵijkBk, so

∑i,jFijFij  =  ∑i,jϵijkϵijlBkBl  =  2 δklBkBl  =  2B2, \sum_{i,j}F_{ij}F^{ij} \;=\; \sum_{i,j}\epsilon^{ijk}\epsilon^{ijl}B^{k}B^{l} \;=\; 2\,\delta^{kl}B^{k}B^{l} \;=\; 2B^{2}, i,j∑​Fij​Fij=i,j∑​ϵijkϵijlBkBl=2δklBkBl=2B2, (2.6.55)

using the contraction identity ϵijkϵijl=2δkl\epsilon^{ijk}\epsilon^{ijl}=2\delta^{kl}ϵijkϵijl=2δkl (sum on i,ji,ji,j), which is the previous identity ϵijkϵklm=δilδjm−δimδjl\epsilon^{ijk}\epsilon^{klm}=\delta^{il}\delta^{jm}-\delta^{im}\delta^{jl}ϵijkϵklm=δilδjm−δimδjl with one more index contracted. Adding:

  FμνFμν  =  2(B2−E2c2).   \boxed{\;F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} \;=\; 2\left(B^{2} - \frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}}\right).\;} Fμν​Fμν=2(B2−c2E2​).​ (2.6.56)

7.2 · The second invariant

The other contraction available uses the Levi-Civita symbol of Chapter 2.4 §8.1:

ϵμνρσFμνFρσ. \epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma}. ϵμνρσ​FμνFρσ. (2.6.57)

Total antisymmetry means the only surviving terms are those in which {μν}\{\mu\nu\}{μν} and {ρσ}\{\rho\sigma\}{ρσ} are complementary pairs. There are three such pair-splittings — {01∣23}\{01|23\}{01∣23}, {02∣13}\{02|13\}{02∣13}, {03∣12}\{03|12\}{03∣12} — and each accounts for eight of the 242424 nonzero permutations: two orderings inside the first pair, two inside the second, and two choices of which pair comes first. Flipping any of those three costs a sign in ϵ\epsilonϵ and a sign in one factor of FFF, so all eight terms are equal. Hence

ϵμνρσFμνFρσ=8[ϵ0123F01F23+ϵ0213F02F13+ϵ0312F03F12]=8[(−Exc)(−Bx)−(−Eyc)(By)+(−Ezc)(−Bz)], \begin{aligned} \epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma} &= 8\Big[\epsilon_{0123}F^{01}F^{23} + \epsilon_{0213}F^{02}F^{13} + \epsilon_{0312}F^{03}F^{12}\Big]\\[3pt] &= 8\left[\left(-\frac{E_{x}}{c}\right)(-B_{x}) - \left(-\frac{E_{y}}{c}\right)(B_{y}) + \left(-\frac{E_{z}}{c}\right)(-B_{z})\right], \end{aligned} ϵμνρσ​FμνFρσ​=8[ϵ0123​F01F23+ϵ0213​F02F13+ϵ0312​F03F12]=8[(−cEx​​)(−Bx​)−(−cEy​​)(By​)+(−cEz​​)(−Bz​)],​ (2.6.58)

using ϵ0123=+1\epsilon_{0123}=+1ϵ0123​=+1, ϵ0213=−1\epsilon_{0213}=-1ϵ0213​=−1 (one transposition) and ϵ0312=+1\epsilon_{0312}=+1ϵ0312​=+1 (two transpositions), together with the entries of (2.6.15). All three terms come out positive:

  ϵμνρσFμνFρσ  =  8c  E⋅B.   \boxed{\;\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma} \;=\; \frac{8}{c}\;\vv E\cdot\vv B.\;} ϵμνρσ​FμνFρσ=c8​E⋅B.​ (2.6.59)
⚑ It is a pseudoscalar, per Chapter 2.4 §8.1

That chapter proved ϵμνρσ′=(det⁡Λ)−1ϵμνρσ\epsilon'_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=(\det\Lambda)^{-1}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}ϵμνρσ′​=(detΛ)−1ϵμνρσ​ and noted that det⁡Λ=±1\det\Lambda=\pm1detΛ=±1 for Lorentz transformations. So (2.6.59) is genuinely invariant under boosts and rotations (det⁡Λ=+1\det\Lambda=+1detΛ=+1) but changes sign under a spatial reflection. It is a pseudoscalar. That is not a defect; it is a fact about E⋅B\vv E\cdot\vv BE⋅B, which is the dot product of a vector with a pseudovector. Chapter 2.4 also flagged, and we re-flag, that for general coordinate changes ϵ\epsilonϵ is a tensor density and needs a factor of −g\sqrt{-g}−g​; within Part II, where det⁡Λ=±1\det\Lambda=\pm1detΛ=±1, that never bites. A term proportional to (2.6.59) may legally be added to the Lagrangian of §9 and is the notorious θ\thetaθ-term; Chapter 6.5 explains why the strong interaction's version of it is measured to be astonishingly close to zero.

7.3 · What the invariants forbid

Two numbers, agreed on by everyone. They are strong constraints, and it is worth being exact about what each rules out.

A plane light wave stays a plane light wave. Chapter 2.1 §2 found that in an electromagnetic wave E⊥B\vv E\perp\vv BE⊥B and E=cBE=cBE=cB. Then both invariants vanish:

B2−E2c2  =  B2−B2  =  0,E⋅B  =  0. B^{2}-\frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}} \;=\; B^{2}-B^{2} \;=\; 0, \qquad\qquad \vv E\cdot\vv B \;=\; 0. B2−c2E2​=B2−B2=0,E⋅B=0. (2.6.60)

Both are zero in every frame, so E′=cB′E'=cB'E′=cB′ and E′⊥B′\vv E'\perp\vv B'E′⊥B′ for every observer, no matter how fast. You may Doppler-shift a light wave to any frequency you like and change its amplitude by any factor — Chapter 2.5 §7.2 computed exactly how — but you can never make it into something other than a light wave. In particular you cannot bring light to rest: a stationary field configuration would have to have E\vv EE and B\vv BB independent, and there is no frame in which the ratio E/cBE/cBE/cB is anything but 111.

When can you kill the magnetic field? Suppose there exists a frame with B′=0\vv B'=\vv 0B′=0. Then in that frame the invariants read −E′2/c2-E'^{2}/c^{2}−E′2/c2 and 000. Since invariants are invariants, that requires

B2−E2c2  <  0(i.e. E>cB),andE⋅B  =  0, B^{2}-\frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}} \;\lt\; 0 \quad\text{(i.e. } E\gt cB\text{)}, \qquad\text{and}\qquad \vv E\cdot\vv B \;=\; 0, B2−c2E2​<0(i.e. E>cB),andE⋅B=0, (2.6.61)

in every frame, in particular in yours. So the condition is checkable without leaving home: the fields must be perpendicular and the electric one must dominate. (These conditions are also sufficient — Worked example 2 constructs the frame explicitly in the mirror-image case.)

When can you kill the electric field? By the identical argument with the roles swapped:

B2−E2c2  >  0(i.e. E<cB),andE⋅B  =  0. B^{2}-\frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}} \;\gt\; 0 \quad\text{(i.e. } E\lt cB\text{)}, \qquad\text{and}\qquad \vv E\cdot\vv B \;=\; 0. B2−c2E2​>0(i.e. E<cB),andE⋅B=0. (2.6.62)

Worked example 2 does this case in full and finds the frame velocity, which turns out to be the drift velocity every mass spectrometer relies on.

And if E⋅B≠0\vv E\cdot\vv B\neq0E⋅B=0, neither field can be removed in any frame, ever. The two fields are then irreducibly both present, and the best you can do is find a frame where they are parallel.

Reading the invariants as a classification

The pair (FμνFμν, ϵFF)\big(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu},\ \epsilon F F\big)(Fμν​Fμν, ϵFF) classifies field configurations into frame-independent types, exactly as the sign of Δs2\Delta s^{2}Δs2 classified pairs of events in Chapter 2.3 into timelike, spacelike and null.

InvariantsNameSimplest frame
E>cBE\gt cBE>cB, E⋅B=0\vv E\cdot\vv B=0E⋅B=0electrica frame with B=0\vv B=\vv 0B=0: pure electrostatics
E<cBE\lt cBE<cB, E⋅B=0\vv E\cdot\vv B=0E⋅B=0magnetica frame with E=0\vv E=\vv 0E=0: pure magnetostatics
E=cBE=cBE=cB, E⋅B=0\vv E\cdot\vv B=0E⋅B=0nullnone simpler — a radiation field
E⋅B≠0\vv E\cdot\vv B\neq0E⋅B=0generica frame with E∥B\vv E\parallel\vv BE∥B

The null case is the boundary between the other two and is exactly the case that cannot be simplified — the same way a null interval sits on the boundary of the light cone and cannot be transformed into either a pure time separation or a pure space separation. Light is the null case of electromagnetism in precisely the sense that a light ray is the null case of a worldline.

That table has a shape. Take E=(E∥,E⊥,0)\vv E=(E_{\parallel},E_{\perp},0)E=(E∥​,E⊥​,0) and B=(B∥,0,B⊥)\vv B=(B_{\parallel},0,B_{\perp})B=(B∥​,0,B⊥​) — a configuration on which a boost along x^\hat{\vv x}x^ closes in two dimensions — and the four rows become four regions of one plane.

In plain terms 2.6.7

Since each field separately depends on who is looking, the quantities worth having are those nobody can dispute, which means whatever survives contracting every label away. From one antisymmetric object there are exactly two such numbers: the difference between the squared magnitudes of the fields, and the amount by which they overlap. Everybody computes the same pair, whatever their motion.

The pair sorts field configurations into types not open to argument, as the sign of the interval sorted pairs of events into three kinds. Where the fields stand perpendicular and the electric one dominates, some observer finds no magnetism at all; where the magnetic dominates, some observer finds no electricity; and where the two are not perpendicular, neither can be removed by anybody ever, the best available simplification being a frame in which they lie parallel. The test is run without leaving home, because the quantities tested are agreed.

Light is the case where both numbers vanish, and since they vanish for everybody, no change of frame turns a light wave into anything else. Its frequency may be shifted to whatever you like and its amplitude scaled by any factor, and it can never be brought to rest, because no frame exists in which the two fields become independent. Light sits at the boundary between the electric and magnetic types exactly as a light ray sits on the boundary of the light cone.

8 · The Lorentz force, covariantly

Chapter 2.5 §6.1 established the shape any relativistic force law must have:

dpμdτ  =  fμ,with the constraintf⋅u  =  0. \dv{p^{\mu}}{\tau} \;=\; f^{\mu}, \qquad\text{with the constraint}\qquad f\cdot u \;=\; 0. dτdpμ​=fμ,with the constraintf⋅u=0. (2.6.63)

What can fμf^{\mu}fμ be for a charge in an electromagnetic field? It must be a four-vector, linear in the charge, and built from the only field object available. With uμu^{\mu}uμ the particle's four-velocity there is essentially one candidate:

  dpμdτ  =  q Fμνuν.   \boxed{\;\dv{p^{\mu}}{\tau} \;=\; q\,F^{\mu\nu}u_{\nu}.\;} dτdpμ​=qFμνuν​.​ (2.6.64)

Chapter 2.4's grind box on the quotient theorem already flagged this: requiring FμνuνF^{\mu\nu}u_{\nu}Fμνuν​ to be a four-vector for every four-velocity is what certifies FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν as a tensor. Now we verify that (2.6.64) is the force law you already know.

8.1 · The spatial components

Lower the index on the four-velocity uμ=γ(c,v)u^{\mu}=\gamma(c,\vv v)uμ=γ(c,v) of Chapter 2.5 §1.3, which flips the sign of the spatial part:

uν  =  ηναuα  =  γ(c, −v). u_{\nu} \;=\; \eta_{\nu\alpha}u^{\alpha} \;=\; \gamma\big(c,\,-\vv v\big). uν​=ηνα​uα=γ(c,−v). (2.6.65)

Take μ=i\mu=iμ=i and split the sum over ν\nuν into its time and space parts:

qFiνuν  =  q[Fi0u0  +  Fijuj]=  q[Eic (γc)  +  (−ϵijkBk)(−γvj)]=  γq[Ei+ϵijkvjBk]  =  γq[E+v×B]i. \begin{aligned} qF^{i\nu}u_{\nu} \;&=\; q\Big[F^{i0}u_{0} \;+\; F^{ij}u_{j}\Big]\\[3pt] &=\; q\left[\frac{E^{i}}{c}\,(\gamma c) \;+\; \big(-\epsilon^{ijk}B^{k}\big)\big(-\gamma v^{j}\big)\right]\\[3pt] &=\; \gamma q\left[E^{i} + \epsilon^{ijk}v^{j}B^{k}\right] \;=\; \gamma q\left[\vv E + \vv v\times\vv B\right]^{i}. \end{aligned} qFiνuν​​=q[Fi0u0​+Fijuj​]=q[cEi​(γc)+(−ϵijkBk)(−γvj)]=γq[Ei+ϵijkvjBk]=γq[E+v×B]i.​ (2.6.66)

The left-hand side is dpi/dτ=γ dpi/dt\dd p^{i}/\dd\tau=\gamma\,\dd p^{i}/\dd tdpi/dτ=γdpi/dt, since dt/dτ=γ\dd t/\dd\tau=\gammadt/dτ=γ (Chapter 2.5 §1.2). Cancel the common γ\gammaγ:

  dpdt  =  q(E+v×B).   \boxed{\;\dv{\vv p}{t} \;=\; q\big(\vv E + \vv v\times\vv B\big).\;} dtdp​=q(E+v×B).​ (2.6.67)

The Lorentz force law — the one Chapter 1.1 §3.3 had to quote, now derived as the spatial part of a four-vector equation. Notice that p=γmv\vv p=\gamma m\vv vp=γmv here, not mvm\vv vmv; the relativistic correction rides along for free.

8.2 · The time component is the power

Take μ=0\mu=0μ=0. The ν=0\nu=0ν=0 term dies because F00=0F^{00}=0F00=0:

qF0νuν  =  qF0juj  =  q(−Ejc)(−γvj)  =  γqc E⋅v. qF^{0\nu}u_{\nu} \;=\; qF^{0j}u_{j} \;=\; q\left(-\frac{E^{j}}{c}\right)\big(-\gamma v^{j}\big) \;=\; \frac{\gamma q}{c}\,\vv E\cdot\vv v. qF0νuν​=qF0juj​=q(−cEj​)(−γvj)=cγq​E⋅v. (2.6.68)

And the left-hand side is dp0/dτ=γ d(E/c)/dt\dd p^{0}/\dd\tau=\gamma\,\dd(E/c)/\dd tdp0/dτ=γd(E/c)/dt, where EEE is now the particle's energy of Chapter 2.5 §3 (an unfortunate clash of symbols that the whole subject lives with). Cancelling γ/c\gamma/cγ/c:

dEdt  =  q E⋅v. \dv{E}{t} \;=\; q\,\vv E\cdot\vv v. dtdE​=qE⋅v. (2.6.69)

The magnetic field does no work. That familiar fact is here not a separate observation but a consequence of where B\vv BB sits in the matrix: the F0jF^{0j}F0j entries are purely electric, so only E\vv EE can appear in the energy equation. And (2.6.69) is Chapter 2.5's work–energy theorem dE/dt=F⋅v\dd E/\dd t=\vv F\cdot\vv vdE/dt=F⋅v with F\vv FF the Lorentz force, since (v×B)⋅v=0(\vv v\times\vv B)\cdot\vv v=0(v×B)⋅v=0 automatically.

8.3 · The constraint is automatic, and why

Chapter 2.5 §6.1 proved that any four-force must satisfy f⋅u=0f\cdot u=0f⋅u=0, because u⋅u=c2u\cdot u=c^{2}u⋅u=c2 is constant. That is a strong condition, and it is not obvious that an arbitrary guess for fμf^{\mu}fμ would satisfy it. Check (2.6.64):

f⋅u  =  fμuμ  =  q Fμνuνuμ  =  0. f\cdot u \;=\; f^{\mu}u_{\mu} \;=\; q\,F^{\mu\nu}u_{\nu}u_{\mu} \;=\; 0. f⋅u=fμuμ​=qFμνuν​uμ​=0. (2.6.70)

Why zero? Because FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν is antisymmetric under μ↔ν\mu\leftrightarrow\nuμ↔ν while uμuνu_{\mu}u_{\nu}uμ​uν​ is symmetric, and a symmetric object fully contracted with an antisymmetric one vanishes. The argument, once, in case it has not been made explicit before: relabel the dummy indices μ↔ν\mu\leftrightarrow\nuμ↔ν in the sum, which changes nothing;

S  ≡  Fμνuμuν  =  Fνμuνuμ  =  −Fμνuμuν  =  −S⟹S=0. S \;\equiv\; F^{\mu\nu}u_{\mu}u_{\nu} \;=\; F^{\nu\mu}u_{\nu}u_{\mu} \;=\; -F^{\mu\nu}u_{\mu}u_{\nu} \;=\; -S \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad S=0. S≡Fμνuμ​uν​=Fνμuν​uμ​=−Fμνuμ​uν​=−S⟹S=0. (2.6.71)
The structural check that had to work

Look at what just happened. The constraint f⋅u=0f\cdot u=0f⋅u=0 is a statement about the geometry of spacetime — it says a four-force can only push a four-velocity sideways, because four-velocities all have the same length. It came from Chapter 2.5 with no reference to electromagnetism whatsoever.

And it is satisfied by (2.6.64) because FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν is antisymmetric — a fact that came from F=∂A−∂AF=\partial A-\partial AF=∂A−∂A, with no reference to spacetime geometry whatsoever. Two independent constraints, from two unrelated directions, matching exactly. Its physical content is (2.6.69): the reason the magnetic force does no work is the reason a four-force is orthogonal to a four-velocity. Had FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν had any symmetric part, charges would gain energy from nothing.

In plain terms 2.6.8

Three requirements and a shortage of materials pin down the force on a charge. It must be a four-part object, proportional to the charge, and assembled out of the particle's four-velocity and the one field object available; essentially one candidate meets all three. Expanding it returns the force law the first part of this book had to quote without justification, with the repaired momentum riding along at no extra cost, while its time entry says the particle's energy changes at the rate the electric field does work.

That the magnetic field does no work is therefore not a separate fact to be remembered. It is a remark about where the magnetic entries sit, since they occupy the purely spatial part of the array and so cannot appear in the equation governing energy. The familiar statement and the arrangement of the object are one thing.

Then a check that had to work, and does. Any four-force must stand perpendicular to the four-velocity, a constraint out of the geometry of the interval with no reference to electricity. The candidate satisfies it because the field tensor reverses sign when its labels are swapped, a property out of the freedom in the potentials with no reference to geometry. Two constraints from unrelated directions, matching exactly. Had the field tensor carried any part that did not reverse sign, charges would gain energy from nothing.

9 · The action

Chapter 1.2 §8.1 listed eight actions and promised each would be constructed in its own chapter. Line three said electromagnetic field, Chapter 2.6. Here it is, with the source term and the SI constants restored:

  LEM  =  −14μ0 FμνFμν  −  jμAμ.   \boxed{\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{EM}} \;=\; -\frac{1}{4\mu_{0}}\,F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} \;-\; j_{\mu}A^{\mu}.\;} LEM​=−4μ0​1​Fμν​Fμν−jμ​Aμ.​ (2.6.72)

Two terms, one line, and it contains every result of §3. The claim to verify is that feeding (2.6.72) to the field Euler–Lagrange equation of Chapter 1.2 §8 returns ∂μFμν=μ0jν\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_{0}j^{\nu}∂μ​Fμν=μ0​jν.

9.1 · Varying it

The dynamical variable is AνA_{\nu}Aν​ — four fields, one for each value of ν\nuν — so the Euler–Lagrange equation carries a free index:

∂μ ⁣(∂L∂(∂μAν))  −  ∂L∂Aν  =  0. \partial_{\mu}\!\left(\pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})}\right) \;-\; \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{A_{\nu}} \;=\; 0. ∂μ​(∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂L​)−∂Aν​∂L​=0. (2.6.73)

The second term is immediate: only −jμAμ=−jνAν-j_{\mu}A^{\mu}=-j^{\nu}A_{\nu}−jμ​Aμ=−jνAν​ contains AνA_{\nu}Aν​ undifferentiated, so ∂L/∂Aν=−jν\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A_{\nu}=-j^{\nu}∂L/∂Aν​=−jν. The first term is the work, and the grind box does it slowly. The answer is

∂L∂(∂μAν)  =  −1μ0Fμν. \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})} \;=\; -\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\nu}. ∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂L​=−μ0​1​Fμν. (2.6.74)

Substituting both into (2.6.73):

∂μ ⁣(−1μ0Fμν)+jν  =  0⟹∂μFμν  =  μ0jν. \partial_{\mu}\!\left(-\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\nu}\right) + j^{\nu} \;=\; 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu} \;=\; \mu_{0}j^{\nu}. ∂μ​(−μ0​1​Fμν)+jν=0⟹∂μ​Fμν=μ0​jν. (2.6.75)

Which is (2.6.19) — Gauss's law and Ampère–Maxwell, both of them, out of one scalar. The homogeneous pair needs no varying at all: it holds identically the moment you write FFF in terms of AAA, which is §3.4.

Grind box — differentiating FαβFαβF_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}Fαβ​Fαβ with respect to ∂μAν\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}∂μ​Aν​

This is pure index gymnastics and it is worth doing once with every step visible, because the same manipulation reappears in Chapters 5.2, 6.3 and 6.4 with more indices.

Step 1 — the chain rule on a product. Write LF=−14μ0FαβFαβ\mathcal{L}_{F}=-\tfrac{1}{4\mu_{0}}F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}LF​=−4μ0​1​Fαβ​Fαβ and note FαβFαβ=ηαγηβδFαβFγδF_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}=\eta^{\alpha\gamma}\eta^{\beta\delta}F_{\alpha\beta}F_{\gamma\delta}Fαβ​Fαβ=ηαγηβδFαβ​Fγδ​, so it is quadratic in the FαβF_{\alpha\beta}Fαβ​ with constant coefficients. Hence

∂∂(∂μAν)(FαβFαβ)  =  2Fαβ ∂Fαβ∂(∂μAν). \pdv{}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})}\big(F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}\big) \;=\; 2F^{\alpha\beta}\,\pdv{F_{\alpha\beta}}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})}. ∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂​(Fαβ​Fαβ)=2Fαβ∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂Fαβ​​.

Step 2 — the inner derivative. Since Fαβ=∂αAβ−∂βAαF_{\alpha\beta}=\partial_{\alpha}A_{\beta}-\partial_{\beta}A_{\alpha}Fαβ​=∂α​Aβ​−∂β​Aα​ and the sixteen quantities ∂μAν\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}∂μ​Aν​ are treated as independent variables,

∂(∂αAβ)∂(∂μAν)  =  δμα δνβ⟹∂Fαβ∂(∂μAν)  =  δμαδνβ−δμβδνα. \pdv{(\partial_{\alpha}A_{\beta})}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})} \;=\; \delta^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\,\delta^{\nu}{}_{\beta} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \pdv{F_{\alpha\beta}}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})} \;=\; \delta^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\delta^{\nu}{}_{\beta} - \delta^{\mu}{}_{\beta}\delta^{\nu}{}_{\alpha}. ∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂(∂α​Aβ​)​=δμα​δνβ​⟹∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂Fαβ​​=δμα​δνβ​−δμβ​δνα​.

The two deltas in each product are what turn "differentiate with respect to a particular component" into "select that component"; the two terms are the two places ∂A\partial A∂A appears in FFF.

Step 3 — contract. The deltas rename indices:

2Fαβ(δμαδνβ−δμβδνα)  =  2(Fμν−Fνμ)  =  4Fμν, 2F^{\alpha\beta}\big(\delta^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\delta^{\nu}{}_{\beta} - \delta^{\mu}{}_{\beta}\delta^{\nu}{}_{\alpha}\big) \;=\; 2\big(F^{\mu\nu} - F^{\nu\mu}\big) \;=\; 4F^{\mu\nu}, 2Fαβ(δμα​δνβ​−δμβ​δνα​)=2(Fμν−Fνμ)=4Fμν,

the last step by antisymmetry — and there is the factor of 444 that the 14\tfrac1441​ in (2.6.72) was put there to cancel. So

∂LF∂(∂μAν)  =  −14μ0⋅4Fμν  =  −1μ0Fμν, \pdv{\mathcal{L}_{F}}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu})} \;=\; -\frac{1}{4\mu_{0}}\cdot 4F^{\mu\nu} \;=\; -\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\nu}, ∂(∂μ​Aν​)∂LF​​=−4μ0​1​⋅4Fμν=−μ0​1​Fμν,

which is (2.6.74). The source term contains no derivatives of AAA and contributes nothing here. ✓

Why the sign of the whole Lagrangian is what it is. Expand (2.6.72) into three-vector language using (2.6.56):

−14μ0FμνFμν  =  −12μ0(B2−E2c2)  =  ϵ0E22−B22μ0. -\frac{1}{4\mu_{0}}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} \;=\; -\frac{1}{2\mu_{0}}\left(B^{2}-\frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}}\right) \;=\; \frac{\epsilon_{0}E^{2}}{2} - \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}. −4μ0​1​Fμν​Fμν=−2μ0​1​(B2−c2E2​)=2ϵ0​E2​−2μ0​B2​.

That is kinetic minus potential — the electric term carries the time derivatives of A\vv AA and plays the role of TTT, the magnetic term carries the spatial derivatives and plays the role of VVV. The overall sign of (2.6.72) is fixed by demanding that TTT come out positive, which is Chapter 1.2 §5's discussion transplanted verbatim to a field. Get it wrong and the field has negative kinetic energy, which Chapter 5.2 shows is a catastrophe rather than a sign convention.

9.2 · Why this Lagrangian and not another

The variation above is a verification, not a derivation: we wrote down (2.6.72) and checked it. So where did it come from? The honest answer is a short list of demands.

  1. Lorentz invariance. L\mathcal{L}L must be a scalar, or the action is not the same number for every observer and the theory has a preferred frame. That immediately restricts us to contractions: FμνFμνF_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}Fμν​Fμν, ϵFF\epsilon FFϵFF, AμAμA_{\mu}A^{\mu}Aμ​Aμ, jμAμj_{\mu}A^{\mu}jμ​Aμ, and products and derivatives of these.
  2. Gauge invariance. L\mathcal{L}L must be unchanged (up to a four-divergence) under (2.6.29). This kills AμAμA_{\mu}A^{\mu}Aμ​Aμ outright — it is not gauge invariant, and it would have been a photon mass term. The photon is massless because a mass term is not gauge invariant. It permits jμAμj_{\mu}A^{\mu}jμ​Aμ only because charge is conserved, as §4.1 showed.
  3. Second-order equations of motion. L\mathcal{L}L should contain at most first derivatives of AAA, so that Euler–Lagrange returns something second order and the initial-value problem is the usual one.
  4. Parity, if you want it. ϵμνρσFμνFρσ\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma}ϵμνρσ​FμνFρσ passes tests 1–3 but is a pseudoscalar, and moreover is a total derivative, so it does not affect the classical field equations at all.

What survives at lowest order is FμνFμνF_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}Fμν​Fμν and jμAμj_{\mu}A^{\mu}jμ​Aμ, with two constants — one of which is fixed by matching Coulomb's law and the other absorbed into the normalisation of AAA. The form is very nearly forced.

Three doors this opens

Chapter 6.4 — Yang–Mills. Take (2.6.72), let AμA^{\mu}Aμ carry an internal index and become matrix-valued, and define Fμν=∂μAν−∂νAμ−ig[Aμ,Aν]F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}A_{\mu}-\ii g[A_{\mu},A_{\nu}]Fμν​=∂μ​Aν​−∂ν​Aμ​−ig[Aμ​,Aν​]. Then write down −12tr⁡FμνFμν-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}−21​trFμν​Fμν — the same expression, entry seven in Chapter 1.2's table. The commutator is the only new ingredient, and it is what makes gluons carry colour charge and interact with each other. The strong and weak interactions are this chapter with a non-commuting symmetry group.

Chapter 5.11 — effective field theory. The argument of §9.2 is the beginning of a general method: list the fields, list the symmetries, write down every term allowed, and order them by how many derivatives they have. The leading term is the theory; the rest are corrections suppressed by powers of energy. Electromagnetism looks fundamental partly because the leading allowed term is so simple. Higher terms exist — (FμνFμν)2\big(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\big)^{2}(Fμν​Fμν)2 is the Euler–Heisenberg term, which makes light scatter off light — and are suppressed by four powers of the electron mass, which is why nobody noticed for a century.

Chapter 5.2 — quantisation. A Lagrangian is the input to a path integral. Once you have (2.6.72), quantising the electromagnetic field is a well-posed problem, and its answer is the photon. The vertex of quantum electrodynamics is the term −jμAμ-j_{\mu}A^{\mu}−jμ​Aμ (Chapter 5.8), which is the entire interaction between light and matter and which you have just written down.

⚠ A note on units, before Part V

The factors of μ0\mu_{0}μ0​, ϵ0\epsilon_{0}ϵ0​ and ccc cluttering this chapter are SI, and they carry real information here: they are what let you compare a derived force against a laboratory measurement in newtons, which §6 and the worked examples do. From Part V onward the book switches to natural units, ℏ=c=1\hbar=c=1ℏ=c=1, in the Heaviside–Lorentz convention where the 4π4\pi4π is moved out of Coulomb's law and ϵ0=μ0=1\epsilon_{0}=\mu_{0}=1ϵ0​=μ0​=1. In those units (2.6.72) reads L=−14FμνFμν−jμAμ\mathcal{L}=-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-j_{\mu}A^{\mu}L=−41​Fμν​Fμν−jμ​Aμ, which is how you will see it written everywhere else, and every equation in this chapter loses its decoration. Nothing physical changes; the constants can always be restored by dimensional analysis. We keep them here because Part II is about measurable consequences and dropping ccc while still learning what ccc means would be perverse.

In plain terms 2.6.9

Compress everything so far and one line is left: one number formed by contracting the field tensor with itself, and one term coupling the current to the potential. Hand that line to the machinery of the first part and out comes the equation saying charges and currents make fields, constants and all. The other half needs no varying, holding the instant the field is written in terms of potentials.

How nearly the form is forced is what to carry away. Demand a number every observer computes alike and only contractions are admitted. Demand that the redundancy in the potentials stay invisible and one candidate is killed outright, the one that would have given the force's carrier a mass, which is the whole reason light has none. Demand no more than first derivatives and almost nothing is left. Two terms survive, their constants fixed by matching the static force and by a choice of normalisation.

The method is worth more than the result. List the ingredients, list the symmetries, write down every term they permit and order these by how many derivatives they carry, whereupon the leading one is the theory and the rest are corrections. Let the potential carry an internal label and become a matrix, add the one ingredient non-commuting labels supply, and the same line written again is the strong interaction, whose carriers act on one another because that ingredient says they must.

10 · Field momentum, and Newton's third law repaired

Chapter 1.1 §3.3 put two moving charges alone in the universe and showed that the total force on them does not vanish. Momentum appeared from nowhere at a computable rate. That chapter offered two escapes — momentum conservation is false, or momentum is stored somewhere that is not a particle — took the second, named the electromagnetic field as the only candidate, and left an IOU. This section pays it, and the payment is exact.

10.1 · The energy–momentum tensor, from Noether

Chapter 1.4 proved that every continuous symmetry yields a conserved current. The symmetry we have not yet used is the most basic one there is: the laws are the same here as there, and now as then — invariance under spacetime translations xμ→xμ+aμx^{\mu}\to x^{\mu}+a^{\mu}xμ→xμ+aμ. Since aμa^{\mu}aμ has four components, we get four conserved currents, one per direction, and they assemble into a rank-2 object.

Run Chapter 1.4 §6's machinery. Under a translation the field changes by δAλ=−aν∂νAλ\delta A_{\lambda}=-a^{\nu}\partial_{\nu}A_{\lambda}δAλ​=−aν∂ν​Aλ​ and the Lagrangian density by δL=−aν∂νL=∂μ(−aνδμνL)\delta\mathcal{L}=-a^{\nu}\partial_{\nu}\mathcal{L}=\partial_{\mu}\big(-a^{\nu}\delta^{\mu}{}_{\nu}\mathcal{L}\big)δL=−aν∂ν​L=∂μ​(−aνδμν​L) — a four-divergence, which is exactly the loosened invariance condition of Chapter 1.4 §1.2. The Noether current for the ν\nuν-th translation is therefore

Tcanμν  =  ∂L∂(∂μAλ) ∂νAλ  −  ημνL  =  −1μ0Fμλ ∂νAλ  +  ημν4μ0FαβFαβ, T^{\mu\nu}_{\text{can}} \;=\; \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}A_{\lambda})}\,\partial^{\nu}A_{\lambda} \;-\; \eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal{L} \;=\; -\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\lambda}\,\partial^{\nu}A_{\lambda} \;+\; \frac{\eta^{\mu\nu}}{4\mu_{0}}F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}, Tcanμν​=∂(∂μ​Aλ​)∂L​∂νAλ​−ημνL=−μ0​1​Fμλ∂νAλ​+4μ0​ημν​Fαβ​Fαβ, (2.6.76)

using (2.6.74) and setting jμ=0j^{\mu}=0jμ=0 (we are asking what the free field carries). It satisfies ∂μTcanμν=0\partial_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}_{\text{can}}=0∂μ​Tcanμν​=0 by Noether's theorem.

And it is wrong in two ways: it is not symmetric in μν\mu\nuμν, and it is not gauge invariant — it contains AλA_{\lambda}Aλ​ bare, so different gauges assign different energy densities to the same physical field. Both defects are fixed by the freedom Chapter 1.4's grind box identified: adding ∂λΣλμν\partial_{\lambda}\Sigma^{\lambda\mu\nu}∂λ​Σλμν with Σ\SigmaΣ antisymmetric in its first two indices changes no conserved charge. Take

Σλμν  =  1μ0FμλAν,antisymmetric in λμ because F is. \Sigma^{\lambda\mu\nu} \;=\; \frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\lambda}A^{\nu}, \qquad\text{antisymmetric in }\lambda\mu\text{ because }F\text{ is}. Σλμν=μ0​1​FμλAν,antisymmetric in λμ because F is. (2.6.77)

Its divergence is, using ∂λFμλ=−∂λFλμ=−μ0jμ=0\partial_{\lambda}F^{\mu\lambda}=-\partial_{\lambda}F^{\lambda\mu}=-\mu_{0}j^{\mu}=0∂λ​Fμλ=−∂λ​Fλμ=−μ0​jμ=0 in the source-free region,

∂λΣλμν  =  1μ0[(∂λFμλ)⏟= 0Aν+Fμλ∂λAν]  =  1μ0Fμλ ∂λAν. \partial_{\lambda}\Sigma^{\lambda\mu\nu} \;=\; \frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\Big[\underbrace{\big(\partial_{\lambda}F^{\mu\lambda}\big)}_{=\,0}A^{\nu} + F^{\mu\lambda}\partial_{\lambda}A^{\nu}\Big] \;=\; \frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\lambda}\,\partial_{\lambda}A^{\nu}. ∂λ​Σλμν=μ0​1​[=0(∂λ​Fμλ)​​Aν+Fμλ∂λ​Aν]=μ0​1​Fμλ∂λ​Aν. (2.6.78)

Add it to (2.6.76) and the two ∂A\partial A∂A terms combine into an FFF:

Tμν  =  −1μ0Fμλ(∂νAλ−∂λAν)⏟= Fνλ  +  ημν4μ0FαβFαβ. T^{\mu\nu} \;=\; -\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}F^{\mu\lambda}\underbrace{\big(\partial^{\nu}A_{\lambda} - \partial_{\lambda}A^{\nu}\big)}_{\textstyle =\,F^{\nu}{}_{\lambda}} \;+\; \frac{\eta^{\mu\nu}}{4\mu_{0}}F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}. Tμν=−μ0​1​Fμλ=Fνλ​(∂νAλ​−∂λ​Aν)​​+4μ0​ημν​Fαβ​Fαβ. (2.6.79)

Since Fνλ=−FλνF^{\nu}{}_{\lambda}=-F_{\lambda}{}^{\nu}Fνλ​=−Fλ​ν, this is

  Tμν  =  1μ0(FμλFλν  +  14ημνFαβFαβ).   \boxed{\;T^{\mu\nu} \;=\; \frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\left(F^{\mu\lambda}F_{\lambda}{}^{\nu} \;+\; \frac{1}{4}\eta^{\mu\nu}F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}\right).\;} Tμν=μ0​1​(FμλFλ​ν+41​ημνFαβ​Fαβ).​ (2.6.80)

Now it is manifestly gauge invariant (only FFF appears), and it is symmetric — check: the first term is ηλρFμλFρν\eta_{\lambda\rho}F^{\mu\lambda}F^{\rho\nu}ηλρ​FμλFρν, and swapping μ↔ν\mu\leftrightarrow\nuμ↔ν together with the dummy relabel λ↔ρ\lambda\leftrightarrow\rhoλ↔ρ returns it, the two minus signs from antisymmetry cancelling. Symmetry is not cosmetic: Chapter 3.6 puts TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν on the right-hand side of Einstein's equation, whose left-hand side is symmetric by construction.

10.2 · What its components are

T00T^{00}T00. Only λ\lambdaλ spatial contributes to F0λFλ0F^{0\lambda}F_{\lambda}{}^{0}F0λFλ​0, and lowering the index costs a minus:

F0λFλ0  =  F0iηijFj0  =  −F0iFi0  =  +∑i(F0i)2  =  E2c2, F^{0\lambda}F_{\lambda}{}^{0} \;=\; F^{0i}\eta_{ij}F^{j0} \;=\; -F^{0i}F^{i0} \;=\; +\sum_{i}\big(F^{0i}\big)^{2} \;=\; \frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}}, F0λFλ​0=F0iηij​Fj0=−F0iFi0=+i∑​(F0i)2=c2E2​, (2.6.81)

using Fi0=−F0iF^{i0}=-F^{0i}Fi0=−F0i and F0i=−Ei/cF^{0i}=-E^{i}/cF0i=−Ei/c. With η00=1\eta^{00}=1η00=1 and (2.6.56) for the second term,

T00  =  1μ0[E2c2+14⋅2(B2−E2c2)]  =  E22μ0c2+B22μ0  =    ϵ0E22+B22μ0   T^{00} \;=\; \frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\left[\frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}} + \frac{1}{4}\cdot2\left(B^{2}-\frac{E^{2}}{c^{2}}\right)\right] \;=\; \frac{E^{2}}{2\mu_{0}c^{2}} + \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}} \;=\; \boxed{\;\frac{\epsilon_{0}E^{2}}{2} + \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}\;} T00=μ0​1​[c2E2​+41​⋅2(B2−c2E2​)]=2μ0​c2E2​+2μ0​B2​=2ϵ0​E2​+2μ0​B2​​ (2.6.82)

using 1/(μ0c2)=ϵ01/(\mu_{0}c^{2})=\epsilon_{0}1/(μ0​c2)=ϵ0​. That is the energy density of the electromagnetic field — the expression you have probably met as a stated fact, here derived as the conserved Noether charge density of time translation, which is what "energy" has meant since Chapter 1.4 §3.1.

T0iT^{0i}T0i. Now η0i=0\eta^{0i}=0η0i=0, so only the first term survives:

F0λFλi  =  F0j ηjk Fki  =  − F0jFji  =  + F0jFij=  (−Ejc)(−ϵijkBk)  =  1c ϵijkEjBk. \begin{aligned} F^{0\lambda}F_{\lambda}{}^{i} \;&=\; F^{0j}\,\eta_{jk}\,F^{ki} \;=\; -\,F^{0j}F^{ji} \;=\; +\,F^{0j}F^{ij}\\[3pt] &=\; \left(-\frac{E^{j}}{c}\right)\left(-\epsilon^{ijk}B^{k}\right) \;=\; \frac{1}{c}\,\epsilon^{ijk}E^{j}B^{k}. \end{aligned} F0λFλ​i​=F0jηjk​Fki=−F0jFji=+F0jFij=(−cEj​)(−ϵijkBk)=c1​ϵijkEjBk.​ (2.6.83)

T0i  =  1μ0c ϵijkEjBk  =  1c[E×Bμ0]i  =  Sic,S  ≡  E×Bμ0. T^{0i} \;=\; \frac{1}{\mu_{0}c}\,\epsilon^{ijk}E^{j}B^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{c}\left[\frac{\vv E\times\vv B}{\mu_{0}}\right]^{i} \;=\; \frac{S^{i}}{c}, \qquad \vv S \;\equiv\; \frac{\vv E\times\vv B}{\mu_{0}}. T0i=μ0​c1​ϵijkEjBk=c1​[μ0​E×B​]i=cSi​,S≡μ0​E×B​. (2.6.84)

  g  =  T0ice^i  =  Sc2  =  ϵ0 E×B.   \boxed{\;\vv g \;=\; \frac{T^{0i}}{c}\hat{\vv e}_{i} \;=\; \frac{\vv S}{c^{2}} \;=\; \epsilon_{0}\,\vv E\times\vv B.\;} g=cT0i​e^i​=c2S​=ϵ0​E×B.​ (2.6.85)

10.3 · The conservation law, with sources

Now restore the charges, because it is the exchange between field and matter that we care about. Take the divergence of (2.6.80):

μ0 ∂μTμν  =  (∂μFμλ)Fλν⏟(1)  +  Fμλ ∂μFλν⏟(2)  +  12Fαβ ∂νFαβ⏟(3). \mu_{0}\,\partial_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu} \;=\; \underbrace{\big(\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\lambda}\big)F_{\lambda}{}^{\nu}}_{(1)} \;+\; \underbrace{F^{\mu\lambda}\,\partial_{\mu}F_{\lambda}{}^{\nu}}_{(2)} \;+\; \underbrace{\tfrac12 F^{\alpha\beta}\,\partial^{\nu}F_{\alpha\beta}}_{(3)}. μ0​∂μ​Tμν=(1)(∂μ​Fμλ)Fλ​ν​​+(2)Fμλ∂μ​Fλ​ν​​+(3)21​Fαβ∂νFαβ​​​. (2.6.86)

Term (1) is the field equation: ∂μFμλ=μ0jλ\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\lambda}=\mu_{0}j^{\lambda}∂μ​Fμλ=μ0​jλ, so it is μ0jλFλν\mu_{0}j^{\lambda}F_{\lambda}{}^{\nu}μ0​jλFλ​ν. Terms (2) and (3) cancel identically, by the Bianchi identity — the grind box does it. So

  ∂μTμν  =  jλFλν  =  − Fνλjλ.   \boxed{\;\partial_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu} \;=\; j_{\lambda}F^{\lambda\nu} \;=\; -\,F^{\nu\lambda}j_{\lambda}.\;} ∂μ​Tμν=jλ​Fλν=−Fνλjλ​.​ (2.6.87)

The right-hand side is not zero, and it should not be: the field is exchanging energy and momentum with the charges. Expand it. For ν=i\nu=iν=i, using j0=cρj_{0}=c\rhoj0​=cρ and jj=−Jjj_{j}=-J^{j}jj​=−Jj,

Fiλjλ  =  Eic(cρ)+(−ϵijkBk)(−Jj)  =  [ρE+J×B]i, F^{i\lambda}j_{\lambda} \;=\; \frac{E^{i}}{c}(c\rho) + \big(-\epsilon^{ijk}B^{k}\big)\big(-J^{j}\big) \;=\; \big[\rho\vv E + \vv J\times\vv B\big]^{i}, Fiλjλ​=cEi​(cρ)+(−ϵijkBk)(−Jj)=[ρE+J×B]i, (2.6.88)

which is the Lorentz force per unit volume — (2.6.67) written for a continuous distribution. Meanwhile the left-hand side, with ∂0=1c∂t\partial_{0}=\tfrac1c\partial_{t}∂0​=c1​∂t​ and T0i=cgiT^{0i}=cg^{i}T0i=cgi, is ∂tgi+∂jTji\partial_{t}g^{i}+\partial_{j}T^{ji}∂t​gi+∂j​Tji. Therefore

∂g∂t  +  ∇⋅T  =  −(ρE+J×B)  =  − fmech, \pdv{\vv g}{t} \;+\; \nabla\cdot\mathsf{T} \;=\; -\big(\rho\vv E + \vv J\times\vv B\big) \;=\; -\,\vv f_{\text{mech}}, ∂t∂g​+∇⋅T=−(ρE+J×B)=−fmech​, (2.6.89)

with T\mathsf{T}T the spatial block TijT^{ij}Tij (the Maxwell stress tensor). Integrate over all space. The middle term becomes a surface integral at infinity by the divergence theorem, and for a system of charges confined to a finite region the fields fall off at least as fast as 1/r21/r^{2}1/r2, so Tij∼1/r4T^{ij}\sim1/r^{4}Tij∼1/r4 while the area grows as r2r^{2}r2: the surface term vanishes. The last term integrates to the total force on the matter, which is dPmech/dt\dd\vv P_{\text{mech}}/\dd tdPmech​/dt. Hence

  ddt(Pmech+Pfield)  =  0,Pfield  =  ϵ0 ⁣∫ ⁣E×B  d3x.   \boxed{\;\dv{}{t}\Big(\vv P_{\text{mech}} + \vv P_{\text{field}}\Big) \;=\; \vv 0, \qquad \vv P_{\text{field}} \;=\; \epsilon_{0}\!\int\!\vv E\times\vv B\;\dd^{3}x.\;} dtd​(Pmech​+Pfield​)=0,Pfield​=ϵ0​∫E×Bd3x.​ (2.6.90)

The ν=0\nu=0ν=0 component of (2.6.87) gives, by the identical route, ∂tu+∇⋅S=−J⋅E\partial_{t}u+\nabla\cdot\vv S=-\vv J\cdot\vv E∂t​u+∇⋅S=−J⋅E — Poynting's theorem: the field energy in a region falls by the flux of S\vv SS out of it plus the work done on the charges inside. The two statements are one four-vector equation.

Grind box — why terms (2) and (3) cancel

Write term (2) with cleaner dummy names, μ→α\mu\to\alphaμ→α and λ→β\lambda\to\betaλ→β:

(2)  =  Fαβ ∂αFβν. (2) \;=\; F^{\alpha\beta}\,\partial_{\alpha}F_{\beta}{}^{\nu}. (2)=Fαβ∂α​Fβ​ν.

Because FαβF^{\alpha\beta}Fαβ is antisymmetric, only the antisymmetric part of whatever it multiplies survives. So we may replace the second factor by half of it minus its α↔β\alpha\leftrightarrow\betaα↔β swap:

(2)  =  12Fαβ(∂αFβν−∂βFαν). (2) \;=\; \tfrac12 F^{\alpha\beta}\big(\partial_{\alpha}F_{\beta}{}^{\nu} - \partial_{\beta}F_{\alpha}{}^{\nu}\big). (2)=21​Fαβ(∂α​Fβ​ν−∂β​Fα​ν).

Now the Bianchi identity (2.6.25), with the third index raised (legitimate: raise it on every term with the same η\etaη):

∂αFβν+∂βFνα+∂νFαβ  =  0. \partial_{\alpha}F_{\beta}{}^{\nu} + \partial_{\beta}F^{\nu}{}_{\alpha} + \partial^{\nu}F_{\alpha\beta} \;=\; 0. ∂α​Fβ​ν+∂β​Fνα​+∂νFαβ​=0.

Use Fνα=−FανF^{\nu}{}_{\alpha}=-F_{\alpha}{}^{\nu}Fνα​=−Fα​ν on the middle term and rearrange:

∂αFβν−∂βFαν  =  − ∂νFαβ. \partial_{\alpha}F_{\beta}{}^{\nu} - \partial_{\beta}F_{\alpha}{}^{\nu} \;=\; -\,\partial^{\nu}F_{\alpha\beta}. ∂α​Fβ​ν−∂β​Fα​ν=−∂νFαβ​.

Substitute:

(2)  =  −12Fαβ ∂νFαβ  =  − (3).■ (2) \;=\; -\tfrac12 F^{\alpha\beta}\,\partial^{\nu}F_{\alpha\beta} \;=\; -\,(3). \qquad\blacksquare (2)=−21​Fαβ∂νFαβ​=−(3).■

Note what did the work: the homogeneous half of Maxwell — the half §3.4 called bookkeeping. It is not decorative after all. Without it TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν would not be conserved, and energy and momentum would not balance.

10.4 · Back to Chapter 1.1

The configuration, unchanged: charge q1q_{1}q1​ at the origin moving with v1=vx^\vv v_{1}=v\hat{\vv x}v1​=vx^; charge q2q_{2}q2​ at r2=dx^\vv r_{2}=d\hat{\vv x}r2​=dx^ — directly ahead of it — moving with v2=vy^\vv v_{2}=v\hat{\vv y}v2​=vy^​. Both in uniform motion at the instant considered.

What 1.1 found. Charge 1 produces no magnetic field directly ahead of itself, so charge 2 feels no magnetic force; charge 2 does produce one at charge 1's location, so charge 1 does. The magnetic residue was

(F12+F21)mag  =  − μ0q1q2v24πd2 y^. \big(\vv F_{12}+\vv F_{21}\big)_{\text{mag}} \;=\; -\,\frac{\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v^{2}}{4\pi d^{2}}\,\hat{\vv y}. (F12​+F21​)mag​=−4πd2μ0​q1​q2​v2​y^​. (2.6.91)

What 1.1 was entitled to drop, and we are not. That chapter said the electric forces "are equal and opposite along the line joining them, so they cancel". True to zeroth order in v/cv/cv/c — and false at order v2/c2v^{2}/c^{2}v2/c2, which is the very order the magnetic residue lives at. Chapter 1.1 was making a qualitative point and the omission cost it nothing; we are about to make a quantitative one, so we need the correction. It is three lines with §5's transformation rules.

Charge 1's field at charge 2. Boost to charge 1's rest frame S′S'S′. The field point (t=0, x=d)(t=0,\ x=d)(t=0, x=d) has x′=γ(d−v⋅0)=γdx'=\gamma(d-v\cdot0)=\gamma dx′=γ(d−v⋅0)=γd, so in S′S'S′ the charge sits at a Coulomb distance γd\gamma dγd and the field there is q1/(4πϵ0γ2d2)q_{1}/(4\pi\epsilon_{0}\gamma^{2}d^{2})q1​/(4πϵ0​γ2d2), pointing along x^\hat{\vv x}x^ — parallel to the boost. By §5, E∥E_{\parallel}E∥​ is unchanged. So

E1(r2)  =  q14πϵ0d2 1γ2  x^. \vv E_{1}(\vv r_{2}) \;=\; \frac{q_{1}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}d^{2}}\,\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}\;\hat{\vv x}. E1​(r2​)=4πϵ0​d2q1​​γ21​x^. (2.6.92)

Charge 2's field at charge 1. Boost to charge 2's rest frame, which moves along y^\hat{\vv y}y^​. The displacement from charge 2 to the origin, −dx^-d\hat{\vv x}−dx^, is perpendicular to that boost, so it is unchanged and the Coulomb distance is ddd. The field is −q2/(4πϵ0d2) x^-q_{2}/(4\pi\epsilon_{0}d^{2})\,\hat{\vv x}−q2​/(4πϵ0​d2)x^ there, and x^\hat{\vv x}x^ is perpendicular to the boost, so by §5 it is multiplied by γ\gammaγ on transforming to the lab:

E2(r1)  =  − q2γ4πϵ0d2  x^. \vv E_{2}(\vv r_{1}) \;=\; -\,\frac{q_{2}\gamma}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}d^{2}}\;\hat{\vv x}. E2​(r1​)=−4πϵ0​d2q2​γ​x^. (2.6.93)

The two electric forces are q2E1(r2)q_{2}\vv E_{1}(\vv r_{2})q2​E1​(r2​) and q1E2(r1)q_{1}\vv E_{2}(\vv r_{1})q1​E2​(r1​), and they no longer cancel: one is weakened by γ−2\gamma^{-2}γ−2 and the other strengthened by γ\gammaγ, because charge 1 is moving along the line joining them and charge 2 is moving across it. Their sum, expanded to order β2\beta^{2}β2 with γ−2=1−β2\gamma^{-2}=1-\beta^{2}γ−2=1−β2 and γ≈1+12β2\gamma\approx1+\tfrac12\beta^{2}γ≈1+21​β2:

(F12+F21)elec=q1q24πϵ0d2(1γ2−γ)x^≈q1q24πϵ0d2(−32β2)x^  =  − 32 μ0q1q2v24πd2 x^, \begin{aligned} \big(\vv F_{12}+\vv F_{21}\big)_{\text{elec}} &= \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}d^{2}}\Big(\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}} - \gamma\Big)\hat{\vv x}\\[3pt] &\approx \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}d^{2}}\Big(-\tfrac32\beta^{2}\Big)\hat{\vv x} \;=\; -\,\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v^{2}}{4\pi d^{2}}\,\hat{\vv x}, \end{aligned} (F12​+F21​)elec​​=4πϵ0​d2q1​q2​​(γ21​−γ)x^≈4πϵ0​d2q1​q2​​(−23​β2)x^=−23​4πd2μ0​q1​q2​v2​x^,​ (2.6.94)

using β2/ϵ0=v2/(c2ϵ0)=μ0v2\beta^{2}/\epsilon_{0}=v^{2}/(c^{2}\epsilon_{0})=\mu_{0}v^{2}β2/ϵ0​=v2/(c2ϵ0​)=μ0​v2. So the third law fails in the x^\hat{\vv x}x^ direction too, and by a larger amount than in y^\hat{\vv y}y^​. The total rate at which mechanical momentum is being created is

dPmechdt  =  − μ0q1q2v24πd2(32x^+y^). \dv{\vv P_{\text{mech}}}{t} \;=\; -\,\frac{\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v^{2}}{4\pi d^{2}}\left(\frac{3}{2}\hat{\vv x} + \hat{\vv y}\right). dtdPmech​​=−4πd2μ0​q1​q2​v2​(23​x^+y^​). (2.6.95)

10.5 · And where it went

Now compute the field momentum. To the order we need, each charge's magnetic field is Ba=va×Ea/c2\vv B_{a}=\vv v_{a}\times\vv E_{a}/c^{2}Ba​=va​×Ea​/c2 (which §5 gives exactly, by boosting a rest frame where B=0\vv B=\vv 0B=0), and each Ea\vv E_{a}Ea​ may be taken as Coulomb, since E×B\vv E\times\vv BE×B is already first order in v/cv/cv/c and corrections to E\vv EE are second. Expand (2.6.90):

Pfield  =  ϵ0 ⁣∫ ⁣(E1+E2)×(B1+B2) d3x. \vv P_{\text{field}} \;=\; \epsilon_{0}\!\int\!\big(\vv E_{1}+\vv E_{2}\big)\times\big(\vv B_{1}+\vv B_{2}\big)\,\dd^{3}x. Pfield​=ϵ0​∫(E1​+E2​)×(B1​+B2​)d3x. (2.6.96)

The two self terms Ea×Ba\vv E_{a}\times\vv B_{a}Ea​×Ba​ depend only on va\vv v_{a}va​, which is constant, so however large they are (and they are infinite — see the caution below) they contribute nothing to dP/dt\dd\vv P/\dd tdP/dt. Keep the cross terms, and use a×(b×c)=b(a⋅c)−c(a⋅b)\vv a\times(\vv b\times\vv c)=\vv b(\vv a\cdot\vv c)-\vv c(\vv a\cdot\vv b)a×(b×c)=b(a⋅c)−c(a⋅b) on each:

Pfieldint  =  ϵ0c2 ⁣∫ ⁣[(v1+v2)(E1 ⁣⋅ ⁣E2)  −  E2(E1 ⁣⋅ ⁣v2)  −  E1(E2 ⁣⋅ ⁣v1)]d3x. \vv P_{\text{field}}^{\text{int}} \;=\; \frac{\epsilon_{0}}{c^{2}}\!\int\!\Big[\big(\vv v_{1}+\vv v_{2}\big)\big(\vv E_{1}\!\cdot\!\vv E_{2}\big) \;-\; \vv E_{2}\big(\vv E_{1}\!\cdot\!\vv v_{2}\big) \;-\; \vv E_{1}\big(\vv E_{2}\!\cdot\!\vv v_{1}\big)\Big]\dd^{3}x. Pfieldint​=c2ϵ0​​∫[(v1​+v2​)(E1​⋅E2​)−E2​(E1​⋅v2​)−E1​(E2​⋅v1​)]d3x. (2.6.97)

Two integrals are needed, and both are elementary (grind box). With d=r2−r1\vv d=\vv r_{2}-\vv r_{1}d=r2​−r1​, d=∣d∣d=\abs{\vv d}d=∣d∣ and n^=d/d\hat{\vv n}=\vv d/dn^=d/d:

∫ ⁣E1 ⁣⋅ ⁣E2  d3x  =  q1q24πϵ02 d,∫ ⁣E1iE2j  d3x  =  q1q28πϵ02 d(δij−ninj). \int\!\vv E_{1}\!\cdot\!\vv E_{2}\;\dd^{3}x \;=\; \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}^{2}\,d}, \qquad\quad \int\! E_{1}^{i}E_{2}^{j}\;\dd^{3}x \;=\; \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{8\pi\epsilon_{0}^{2}\,d}\Big(\delta^{ij}-n^{i}n^{j}\Big). ∫E1​⋅E2​d3x=4πϵ02​dq1​q2​​,∫E1i​E2j​d3x=8πϵ02​dq1​q2​​(δij−ninj). (2.6.98)

Substitute. Write V≡v1+v2\vv V\equiv\vv v_{1}+\vv v_{2}V≡v1​+v2​; the two tensor terms combine, using the symmetry of Mij≡∫E1iE2j d3xM^{ij}\equiv\int E_{1}^{i}E_{2}^{j}\,\dd^{3}xMij≡∫E1i​E2j​d3x, into MijVjM^{ij}V^{j}MijVj, and the prefactors collapse with 1/(ϵ0c2)=μ01/(\epsilon_{0}c^{2})=\mu_{0}1/(ϵ0​c2)=μ0​:

Pfieldint=ϵ0c2⋅q1q24πϵ02d[V−12(V−n^(n^ ⁣⋅ ⁣V))]=  μ0q1q28πd[V+n^(n^ ⁣⋅ ⁣V)].   \begin{aligned} \vv P_{\text{field}}^{\text{int}} &= \frac{\epsilon_{0}}{c^{2}}\cdot\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}^{2}d}\left[\vv V - \tfrac12\Big(\vv V - \hat{\vv n}\big(\hat{\vv n}\!\cdot\!\vv V\big)\Big)\right]\\[4pt] &= \boxed{\;\frac{\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}}{8\pi d}\Big[\vv V + \hat{\vv n}\big(\hat{\vv n}\!\cdot\!\vv V\big)\Big].\;} \end{aligned} Pfieldint​​=c2ϵ0​​⋅4πϵ02​dq1​q2​​[V−21​(V−n^(n^⋅V))]=8πdμ0​q1​q2​​[V+n^(n^⋅V)].​​ (2.6.99)

For the configuration at hand, at the instant t=0t=0t=0: n^=x^\hat{\vv n}=\hat{\vv x}n^=x^, V=v(x^+y^)\vv V=v(\hat{\vv x}+\hat{\vv y})V=v(x^+y^​), n^⋅V=v\hat{\vv n}\cdot\vv V=vn^⋅V=v, so

Pfield  =  μ0q1q2v8πd(2x^+y^)  ≠  0. \vv P_{\text{field}} \;=\; \frac{\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v}{8\pi d}\big(2\hat{\vv x}+\hat{\vv y}\big) \;\neq\; \vv 0. Pfield​=8πdμ0​q1​q2​v​(2x^+y^​)=0. (2.6.100)

There is momentum in the empty space between the charges. Now differentiate. The separation vector evolves as d(t)=(d−vt)x^+vt y^\vv d(t)=(d-vt)\hat{\vv x}+vt\,\hat{\vv y}d(t)=(d−vt)x^+vty^​, since charge 1 moves +x+x+x and charge 2 moves +y+y+y; at t=0t=0t=0 this gives d˙=−v\dot d=-vd˙=−v and n^˙=(v/d)y^\dot{\hat{\vv n}}=(v/d)\hat{\vv y}n^˙=(v/d)y^​. Grinding through the product rule (grind box):

dPfielddt∣t=0  =  μ0q1q2v24πd2(32x^+y^). \dv{\vv P_{\text{field}}}{t}\bigg|_{t=0} \;=\; \frac{\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v^{2}}{4\pi d^{2}}\left(\frac{3}{2}\hat{\vv x} + \hat{\vv y}\right). dtdPfield​​​t=0​=4πd2μ0​q1​q2​v2​(23​x^+y^​). (2.6.101)

Compare with (2.6.95). Term by term, including the awkward 32\tfrac3223​ that Chapter 1.1 never saw:

  dPmechdt  +  dPfielddt  =  0.   \boxed{\;\dv{\vv P_{\text{mech}}}{t} \;+\; \dv{\vv P_{\text{field}}}{t} \;=\; \vv 0.\;} dtdPmech​​+dtdPfield​​=0.​ (2.6.102)
The longest-running promise in the book, closed

Chapter 1.1 §3.3 wrote down a momentum non-conservation of −μ0q1q2v2y^/4πd2-\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v^{2}\hat{\vv y}/4\pi d^{2}−μ0​q1​q2​v2y^​/4πd2 and offered you a choice: abandon momentum conservation, or accept that the field is a physical object with momentum of its own. The second was right, and now it is computed: the missing momentum is (2.6.100), it lives in the field, and its rate of change is exactly minus the rate at which the particles are gaining momentum from nowhere — in both components, with the 32\tfrac3223​ that only shows up if you are honest about the electric forces at order v2/c2v^{2}/c^{2}v2/c2.

Notice how the repair works. Newton's third law presumed that all the momentum in the universe is carried by particles and that they exchange it instantaneously. Relativity forbids the second clause, and the first then cannot survive: if charge 1 moves now and charge 2 will not know for d/cd/cd/c seconds, the momentum has to be somewhere during the interval. The third law is not a fundamental principle that electromagnetism violates. It is a low-velocity approximation to a four-vector conservation law, and it fails exactly where the approximation does.

The conceptual bill is large and worth paying explicitly. A field can no longer be read as a bookkeeping device — a table of where the force would be if you put a test charge there. Something that stores energy, stores momentum, exerts stresses, and can carry momentum across a room during the interval when neither particle has it, is not a table. It is a physical system with its own degrees of freedom and its own dynamics. That is why Part V quantises it, and why the resulting quanta — photons — are as real as electrons rather than being a way of talking about electrons.

⚠ Two honest cautions

The self terms are infinite. ϵ0∫Ea×Ba d3x\epsilon_{0}\int\vv E_{a}\times\vv B_{a}\,\dd^{3}xϵ0​∫Ea​×Ba​d3x diverges at the location of a point charge, as does the self-energy ϵ02∫Ea2\tfrac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}\int E_{a}^{2}2ϵ0​​∫Ea2​. We dodged it above by noting that these terms are constant when va\vv v_{a}va​ is, so they drop out of the rate. That dodge is legitimate here and evasive in general: the divergence is the classical electron self-energy problem, it is genuinely unsolved in classical physics, and it is the ancestor of the renormalisation programme of Chapter 5.11. Point charges are an idealisation and they bite.

What we computed and what we did not. The general theorem (2.6.90) is exact, derived from ∂μTμν\partial_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}∂μ​Tμν with no approximation. The two-charge check keeps the velocity-dependent terms to order v2/c2v^{2}/c^{2}v2/c2 and drops the acceleration (radiation) fields, whose contribution is balanced separately against the v˙\dot{\vv v}v˙ terms in (2.6.99) — a second, independent piece of bookkeeping controlled by a different small parameter, the ratio of the charges' Coulomb energy to their kinetic energy. Nothing was assumed to make (2.6.102) come out; every coefficient was computed and then compared.

Grind box — the two field integrals of (2.6.98)

Both are done with the same two moves: integrate by parts, then use Gauss's law ∇⋅Ea=ρa/ϵ0\nabla\cdot\vv E_{a}=\rho_{a}/\epsilon_{0}∇⋅Ea​=ρa​/ϵ0​ with ρa=qaδ3(x−ra)\rho_{a}=q_{a}\delta^{3}(\vv x-\vv r_{a})ρa​=qa​δ3(x−ra​). Surface terms vanish because the fields fall off as 1/r21/r^{2}1/r2 and the integrands as 1/r31/r^{3}1/r3 or faster.

The scalar one. Write E1=−∇ϕ1\vv E_{1}=-\nabla\phi_{1}E1​=−∇ϕ1​ and integrate by parts:

∫ ⁣E1 ⁣⋅ ⁣E2 d3x=− ⁣∫ ⁣∇ϕ1⋅E2 d3x=∫ ⁣ϕ1 (∇ ⁣⋅ ⁣E2) d3x=q2ϵ0 ϕ1(r2)=q1q24πϵ02d. \int\!\vv E_{1}\!\cdot\!\vv E_{2}\,\dd^{3}x = -\!\int\!\nabla\phi_{1}\cdot\vv E_{2}\,\dd^{3}x = \int\!\phi_{1}\,\big(\nabla\!\cdot\!\vv E_{2}\big)\,\dd^{3}x = \frac{q_{2}}{\epsilon_{0}}\,\phi_{1}(\vv r_{2}) = \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}^{2}d}. ∫E1​⋅E2​d3x=−∫∇ϕ1​⋅E2​d3x=∫ϕ1​(∇⋅E2​)d3x=ϵ0​q2​​ϕ1​(r2​)=4πϵ02​dq1​q2​​.

Total.

Where TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν goes next

You have built a symmetric, conserved, traceless rank-2 tensor whose 000000 component is energy density and whose 0i0i0i components are momentum density. Chapter 3.6 will take Einstein's field equation

Gμν  =  8πGc4 Tμν G^{\mu\nu} \;=\; \frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}\,T^{\mu\nu} Gμν=c48πG​Tμν

and put this object on the right-hand side. That is what "energy gravitates" means technically: not mass but TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν sources spacetime curvature, so the electromagnetic field itself — light, a magnetic field, the energy in a capacitor — gravitates, with a strength you can now compute. It is also why the equation had to be symmetric in μν\mu\nuμν, which is why §10.1's improvement term was not optional. And the tracelessness ημνTμν=0\eta_{\mu\nu}T^{\mu\nu}=0ημν​Tμν=0, which you can verify in one line from (2.6.80), is the statement that the photon is massless, and reappears in Chapter 5.11 as the conformal symmetry of classical electromagnetism — a symmetry that quantum corrections break.

In plain terms 2.6.10

The oldest debt in the book is settled by computation rather than assertion. Two charges in uniform motion, alone in the universe, were seen in the first part to push on each other unequally, momentum appearing from nowhere. Work out what the empty space between them holds and differentiate: the field loses momentum at exactly the rate the particles gain it, awkward factor of three halves and all.

The diagnosis matters more than the arithmetic. The third law assumed all momentum belongs to particles, handed over the instant either moves. Relativity forbids the second clause: once one charge moves and the other cannot learn of it until light crosses the gap, the momentum must be somewhere meanwhile. What holds it there is no table of where a force would be but a physical system with its own degrees of freedom, which is why a later part must quantise it.

Part II has done its work. You hold a geometry where one speed is the same for everybody with nothing to measure it against, a language making frame-independence visible in an equation's shape, a mechanics of four-entry objects, which is where energy came from, and one field with electricity and magnetism as its slices. One thing has not moved: gravity is still a force reaching across empty space, arriving the moment it is sent, and nothing in this part permits an influence with no delay.

B′=γ(B0−vc2E0)=γB0(1−E02B02c2)=B0γ=B02−E02c2, B' = \gamma\left(B_{0} - \frac{v}{c^{2}}E_{0}\right) = \gamma B_{0}\left(1-\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{B_{0}^{2}c^{2}}\right) = \frac{B_{0}}{\gamma} = \sqrt{B_{0}^{2}-\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{c^{2}}}, B′=γ(B0​−c2v​E0​)=γB0​(1−B02​c2E02​​)=γB0​​=B02​−c2E02​​​,

A charge in a pure magnetic field feels a force always perpendicular to its velocity, does no work ((2.6.69)), and therefore moves in a circle at constant speed, the cyclotron gyration.

Back in the lab, that circle is being carried along at vdrift\vv v_{\text{drift}}vdrift​: the trajectory is a cycloid-like drift, and — this is the point — the drift velocity does not depend on the charge, the sign of the charge, or the mass. Every particle drifts at E×B/B2\vv E\times\vv B/B^{2}E×B/B2.

Why every mass spectrometer contains one. Turn the argument around. A particle that enters crossed fields moving at exactly vdrift\vv v_{\text{drift}}vdrift​ is, in the primed frame, at rest — and a charge at rest in a pure magnetic field feels no force at all. So it passes through undeflected, while anything faster or slower is bent aside. That is a velocity selector: a slit, two plates, a magnet, and one equation. It selects v=E/Bv=E/Bv=E/B regardless of mass and charge, which is exactly what you want in front of a mass analyser that will then separate by m/qm/qm/q. The same E×B\vv E\times\vv BE×B drift governs charged particles in the magnetosphere, the confinement of tokamak plasmas, and the Hall effect.

The pancake. As γ→∞\gamma\to\inftyγ→∞ the forward field dies like 1/γ21/\gamma^{2}1/γ2 while the broadside field grows like γ\gammaγ. Problem 2 — a plane wave has nothing to give up

For a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum, E⊥B\vv E\perp\vv BE⊥B and E=cBE=cBE=cB. Show that both invariants of §7 vanish. Then use that to prove three things: no boost can eliminate either field; no boost can make the fields non-perpendicular; and no boost can bring the wave to rest. What can a boost do to a light wave?

Solution

The invariants. FμνFμν=2(B2−E2/c2)=2(B2−B2)=0F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=2(B^{2}-E^{2}/c^{2})=2(B^{2}-B^{2})=0Fμν​Fμν=2(B2−E2/c2)=2(B2−B2)=0, and ϵμνρσFμνFρσ=(8/c)E⋅B=0\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma}=(8/c)\vv E\cdot\vv B=0ϵμνρσ​FμνFρσ=(8/c)E⋅B=0 since the fields are perpendicular. Both are zero. By the invariance theorem they are zero in every frame.

(i) Neither field can be eliminated. Suppose some frame had B′=0\vv B'=\vv 0B′=0. Then in that frame FμνFμν=−2E′2/c2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=-2E'^{2}/c^{2}Fμν​Fμν=−2E′2/c2, which must equal zero, forcing E′=0E'=0E′=0 as well. So the only way to lose the magnetic field is to lose the whole wave — and you cannot, since a tensor that vanishes in one frame vanishes in all (Chapter 2.4 §6), so a wave that exists at all exists for everyone. Identically for E′=0\vv E'=\vv 0E′=0.

(ii) The fields stay perpendicular and stay in ratio. E′⋅B′=0\vv E'\cdot\vv B'=0E′⋅B′=0 in every frame because the pseudoscalar is invariant, and E′=cB′E'=cB'E′=cB′ in every frame because the scalar is. A light wave looks like a light wave to everybody.

(iii) It cannot be brought to rest. "At rest" would mean a static field configuration, for which E\vv EE and B\vv BB are independent and generically E≠cBE\neq cBE=cB. More sharply: the wave's four-wavevector kμ=(ω/c,k)k^{\mu}=(\omega/c,\vv k)kμ=(ω/c,k) satisfies k⋅k=0k\cdot k=0k⋅k=0 (Chapter 2.5 §7.1), and a null four-vector cannot be boosted to a purely timelike one — that is the same statement as "Δs2=0\Delta s^{2}=0Δs2=0 is preserved" in Chapter 2.3. The vanishing of both field invariants is the field-theoretic face of the same fact: null is a Lorentz-invariant category.

What a boost can do. Change the amplitude and the frequency, together and in the same ratio. From §5, boosting along the propagation direction multiplies both E⊥\vv E_{\perp}E⊥​ and B⊥\vv B_{\perp}B⊥​ by the Doppler factor (1−β)/(1+β)\sqrt{(1-\beta)/(1+\beta)}(1−β)/(1+β)​, exactly the factor Chapter 2.5 §7.2 derived for ω\omegaω. So a light wave can be made as weak and as red as you like — asymptotically, but never exactly, zero. It can also be aimed differently: a boost transverse to k\vv kk changes the propagation direction, which is aberration. What survives every boost is the wave's identity as a wave.

The physical moral. The vanishing of both invariants is what makes light structurally different from every static field. It is also why the photon is massless: the null condition on kμk^{\mu}kμ is E=pcE=pcE=pc (Chapter 2.5 §4.3), and m=0m=0m=0.

Problem 3 — charge conservation as an output, not an input

Show that ∂ν∂μFμν=0\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=0∂ν​∂μ​Fμν=0 identically, for any antisymmetric FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν. Deduce that ∂νjν=0\partial_{\nu}j^{\nu}=0∂ν​jν=0 follows from the field equation rather than being an extra assumption. Then explain what this says about a hypothetical universe in which charge is not conserved, and connect it to Chapter 0.7's Problem 4 on the displacement current.

Solution

The identity. The object ∂ν∂μ\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}∂ν​∂μ​ is symmetric under μ↔ν\mu\leftrightarrow\nuμ↔ν (mixed partials commute) and FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν is antisymmetric. Contracting a symmetric object with an antisymmetric one over both indices gives zero — the argument of (2.6.71), repeated. Explicitly, relabel the two dummy indices:

X≡∂ν∂μFμν=∂μ∂νFνμ=−∂ν∂μFμν=−X  ⟹  X=0. X \equiv \partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu} = \partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}F^{\nu\mu} = -\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu} = -X \;\Longrightarrow\; X=0. X≡∂ν​∂μ​Fμν=∂μ​∂ν​Fνμ=−∂ν​∂μ​Fμν=−X⟹X=0.

The consequence. Take ∂ν\partial_{\nu}∂ν​ of the field equation (2.6.19):

0=∂ν∂μFμν=μ0 ∂νjν⟹∂νjν=0. 0 = \partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu} = \mu_{0}\,\partial_{\nu}j^{\nu} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \partial_{\nu}j^{\nu} = 0. 0=∂ν​∂μ​Fμν=μ0​∂ν​jν⟹∂ν​jν=0.

Charge conservation is a theorem, not a postulate. Section 1 assumed it in order to build jμj^{\mu}jμ; the theory then hands it back.

What it forbids. This is stronger than it looks. It says you cannot write down a consistent electrodynamics with a non-conserved source. If someone hands you a jμj^{\mu}jμ with ∂νjν≠0\partial_{\nu}j^{\nu}\neq0∂ν​jν=0, the equation ∂μFμν=μ0jν\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_{0}j^{\nu}∂μ​Fμν=μ0​jν has no solutions at all — not "solutions with strange behaviour", none. A universe in which charge could appear from nowhere could not have Maxwell's equations, in any frame, even approximately. The rigidity comes entirely from the antisymmetry of FFF, which came from gauge invariance (the callout at the end of §2), which is why Chapter 6.3 can say that gauge symmetry and charge conservation are two descriptions of one fact.

The displacement current. Chapter 0.7's Problem 4 asked you to show that ∇×B=μ0J\nabla\times\vv B=\mu_{0}\vv J∇×B=μ0​J is inconsistent with charge conservation, because taking the divergence gives 0=μ0∇⋅J0=\mu_{0}\nabla\cdot\vv J0=μ0​∇⋅J, which contradicts (2.6.1) whenever ∂tρ≠0\partial_{t}\rho\neq0∂t​ρ=0 — and that the unique minimal repair is Maxwell's μ0ϵ0∂tE\mu_{0}\epsilon_{0}\partial_{t}\vv Eμ0​ϵ0​∂t​E. This problem is the four-dimensional version of that argument, and it is now visibly the same argument: the three-dimensional identity ∇⋅(∇×B)=0\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\vv B)=0∇⋅(∇×B)=0 that forced the repair is the spatial part of ∂ν∂μFμν=0\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=0∂ν​∂μ​Fμν=0. In the covariant formulation the displacement current is not a repair. It was never absent.

Problem 4 — two parallel wires, both ways

Two long parallel wires a distance ddd apart carry currents I1I_{1}I1​ and I2I_{2}I2​ in the same direction. Model each as in §6: lattice +λ0+\lambda_{0}+λ0​ at rest, electrons −λ0-\lambda_{0}−λ0​ drifting at −vax^-v_{a}\hat{\vv x}−va​x^, so that Ia=λ0vaI_{a}=\lambda_{0}v_{a}Ia​=λ0​va​. (a) Compute the force per unit length magnetically, in the lab. (b) Now boost to the rest frame of wire 2's conduction electrons and recompute it electrostatically, being careful about how "per unit length" transforms. (c) Check that wire 2's lattice feels no net force in that frame either, as it must not. (d) Put in I1=I2=1 AI_{1}=I_{2}=1\ \mathrm{A}I1​=I2​=1 A and d=1 cmd=1\ \mathrm{cm}d=1 cm.

Solution

(a) The lab. Wire 1 produces B1=μ0I12πdz^\vv B_{1}=\dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{1}}{2\pi d}\hat{\vv z}B1​=2πdμ0​I1​​z^ at wire 2 (taking wire 2 to lie in the +y^+\hat{\vv y}+y^​ direction from wire 1). Only wire 2's electrons move, with charge per unit length −λ0-\lambda_{0}−λ0​ and velocity −v2x^-v_{2}\hat{\vv x}−v2​x^:

fL=(−λ0)(−v2x^)×μ0I12πdz^=λ0v2μ0I12πd(x^×z^)=−μ0I1I22πd y^. \frac{\vv f}{L} = (-\lambda_{0})(-v_{2}\hat{\vv x})\times\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}}{2\pi d}\hat{\vv z} = \lambda_{0}v_{2}\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}}{2\pi d}\big(\hat{\vv x}\times\hat{\vv z}\big) = -\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}\,\hat{\vv y}. Lf​=(−λ0​)(−v2​x^)×2πdμ0​I1​​z^=λ0​v2​2πdμ0​I1​​(x^×z^)=−2πdμ0​I1​I2​​y^​.

Attractive, magnitude μ0I1I2/2πd\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}/2\pi dμ0​I1​I2​/2πd. The lattice of wire 2 is at rest and wire 1 is neutral, so nothing else contributes.

(b) The co-moving frame. Boost at w=−v2w=-v_{2}w=−v2​ (so wire 2's electrons are at rest). By (2.6.45) with u→wu\to wu→w, wire 1 acquires

λ1′=−γ2λ0wv1c2=+γ2λ0v1v2c2=+γ2I1v2c2,γ2=(1−v22c2)−1/2, \lambda'_{1} = -\gamma_{2}\lambda_{0}\frac{wv_{1}}{c^{2}} = +\gamma_{2}\frac{\lambda_{0}v_{1}v_{2}}{c^{2}} = +\gamma_{2}\frac{I_{1}v_{2}}{c^{2}}, \qquad \gamma_{2}=\Big(1-\frac{v_{2}^{2}}{c^{2}}\Big)^{-1/2}, λ1′​=−γ2​λ0​c2wv1​​=+γ2​c2λ0​v1​v2​​=+γ2​c2I1​v2​​,γ2​=(1−c2v22​​)−1/2,

a positive charge density — and wire 2's electrons are negative, so the force is attractive, agreeing with (a) in direction.

Wire 2's electrons are now at rest, so their density is their proper density, −λ0/γ2-\lambda_{0}/\gamma_{2}−λ0​/γ2​ (they were contracted by γ2\gamma_{2}γ2​ in the lab). The electric field from wire 1 at distance ddd is Ey′=λ1′/2πϵ0dE'_{y}=\lambda'_{1}/2\pi\epsilon_{0}dEy′​=λ1′​/2πϵ0​d, so the force per unit length measured in this frame is

fy′L′=(−λ0γ2)γ2λ0v1v2/c22πϵ0d=−λ02v1v22πϵ0c2d=−μ0I1I22πd. \frac{f'_{y}}{L'} = \left(-\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\gamma_{2}}\right)\frac{\gamma_{2}\lambda_{0}v_{1}v_{2}/c^{2}}{2\pi\epsilon_{0}d} = -\frac{\lambda_{0}^{2}v_{1}v_{2}}{2\pi\epsilon_{0}c^{2}d} = -\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}. L′fy′​​=(−γ2​λ0​​)2πϵ0​dγ2​λ0​v1​v2​/c2​=−2πϵ0​c2dλ02​v1​v2​​=−2πdμ0​I1​I2​​.

The "per unit length" bookkeeping. That looks like the same number as (a), which would be wrong, because transverse forces are not equal in the two frames — they differ by γ\gammaγ ((2.6.48)). The resolution is that lengths differ too. Take a lab segment of length LLL containing NNN electrons. Those same electrons are at rest in the primed frame, so they occupy L′=γ2LL'=\gamma_{2}LL′=γ2​L there. Hence the total force on them is

Fy′=fy′L′⋅L′=−μ0I1I22πd γ2L⟹Fy=Fy′γ2=−μ0I1I22πd L.✓ F'_{y} = \frac{f'_{y}}{L'}\cdot L' = -\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}\,\gamma_{2}L \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F_{y} = \frac{F'_{y}}{\gamma_{2}} = -\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}\,L. \quad\checkmark Fy′​=L′fy′​​⋅L′=−2πdμ0​I1​I2​​γ2​L⟹Fy​=γ2​Fy′​​=−2πdμ0​I1​I2​​L.✓

The two factors of γ2\gamma_{2}γ2​ — one from length contraction, one from force transformation — cancel, which is exactly why the force per unit length happens to come out numerically the same in both frames. That coincidence is worth noticing precisely so that you do not mistake it for a proof; the total force on a given set of charges is the frame-covariant statement.

(c) The lattice of wire 2. In the primed frame it moves at +v2x^+v_{2}\hat{\vv x}+v2​x^, has density γ2λ0\gamma_{2}\lambda_{0}γ2​λ0​, and sits in both an electric and a magnetic field. From §5, Bz′=γ2(Bz−wEy/c2)=γ2μ0I1/2πdB'_{z}=\gamma_{2}(B_{z}-wE_{y}/c^{2})=\gamma_{2}\mu_{0}I_{1}/2\pi dBz′​=γ2​(Bz​−wEy​/c2)=γ2​μ0​I1​/2πd since Ey=0E_{y}=0Ey​=0 in the lab. So

electric:(γ2λ0)γ2λ0v1v2/c22πϵ0d y^=+γ22μ0I1I22πdy^,magnetic:(γ2λ0)(v2x^)×(γ2μ0I12πdz^)=−γ22μ0I1I22πdy^. \begin{aligned} \text{electric:}\quad &(\gamma_{2}\lambda_{0})\frac{\gamma_{2}\lambda_{0}v_{1}v_{2}/c^{2}}{2\pi\epsilon_{0}d}\,\hat{\vv y} = +\gamma_{2}^{2}\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}\hat{\vv y},\\[3pt] \text{magnetic:}\quad &(\gamma_{2}\lambda_{0})(v_{2}\hat{\vv x})\times\Big(\gamma_{2}\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}}{2\pi d}\hat{\vv z}\Big) = -\gamma_{2}^{2}\frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}\hat{\vv y}. \end{aligned} electric:magnetic:​(γ2​λ0​)2πϵ0​dγ2​λ0​v1​v2​/c2​y^​=+γ22​2πdμ0​I1​I2​​y^​,(γ2​λ0​)(v2​x^)×(γ2​2πdμ0​I1​​z^)=−γ22​2πdμ0​I1​I2​​y^​.​

They cancel exactly. The lattice feels nothing, as it must, since in the lab it feels nothing and "zero force" is a frame-independent statement. Notice how the cancellation works: in this frame the lattice is a current, and the repulsion from the now-charged wire 1 is precisely balanced by the magnetic attraction between the two currents. Neither description is more true.

(d) Numbers.

FL=μ0I1I22πd=(4π×10−7)(1)(1)2π(0.01)=2×10−5 N m−1. \frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1)(1)}{2\pi(0.01)} = 2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}. LF​=2πdμ0​I1​I2​​=2π(0.01)(4π×10−7)(1)(1)​=2×10−5 Nm−1.

Twenty micronewtons per metre — small, but measurable with a torsion balance, and until 2019 this configuration defined the ampere: the current which, in two infinite parallel wires one metre apart, produces a force of 2×10−7 N m−12\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}2×10−7 Nm−1. An entire base unit of the SI was defined by a relativistic correction to Coulomb's law of relative order 10−2610^{-26}10−26.

The brick you just laid

Six objects, and Part II is finished.

The four-current jμ=(cρ,J)j^{\mu}=(c\rho,\vv J)jμ=(cρ,J), built by requiring ∂μjμ=0\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0∂μ​jμ=0 to reproduce Chapter 0.7's continuity equation — after which charge conservation is one contracted index and therefore true in every frame. The field tensor Fμν=∂μAν−∂νAμF^{\mu\nu}=\partial^{\mu}A^{\nu}-\partial^{\nu}A^{\mu}Fμν=∂μAν−∂νAμ, whose six independent components are −E/c-\vv E/c−E/c in the first row and −ϵijkBk-\epsilon^{ijk}B^{k}−ϵijkBk in the spatial block — the six that Chapter 2.4 §7.2 counted and promised. Maxwell's four equations as two: ∂μFμν=μ0jν\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_{0}j^{\nu}∂μ​Fμν=μ0​jν expanding to Gauss and Ampère–Maxwell, and ∂[λFμν]=0\partial_{[\lambda}F_{\mu\nu]}=0∂[λ​Fμν]​=0 expanding to ∇⋅B=0\nabla\cdot\vv B=0∇⋅B=0 and Faraday — the second of which is not physics at all but six terms cancelling by Clairaut, which is Chapter 0.7's ∇⋅(∇×A)=0\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\vv A)=0∇⋅(∇×A)=0 and ∇×∇ϕ=0\nabla\times\nabla\phi=\vv 0∇×∇ϕ=0 fused into one identity. Gauge freedom Aμ→Aμ+∂μχA^{\mu}\to A^{\mu}+\partial^{\mu}\chiAμ→Aμ+∂μχ, Chapter 1.2's total-derivative freedom in field form, spent on the Lorenz gauge to give □Aμ=μ0jμ\Box A^{\mu}=\mu_{0}j^{\mu}□Aμ=μ0​jμ. Two invariants, 2(B2−E2/c2)2(B^{2}-E^{2}/c^{2})2(B2−E2/c2) and (8/c)E⋅B(8/c)\vv E\cdot\vv B(8/c)E⋅B, which classify field configurations the way the sign of Δs2\Delta s^{2}Δs2 classifies intervals. The Lagrangian −14μ0FμνFμν−jμAμ-\tfrac{1}{4\mu_{0}}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-j_{\mu}A^{\mu}−4μ0​1​Fμν​Fμν−jμ​Aμ, entry three in Chapter 1.2's table, which on variation returns the field equations and which Chapter 6.4 will copy verbatim with a non-abelian FFF. And the energy–momentum tensor, whose T00T^{00}T00 is 12(ϵ0E2+B2/μ0)\tfrac12(\epsilon_{0}E^{2}+B^{2}/\mu_{0})21​(ϵ0​E2+B2/μ0​) and whose T0iT^{0i}T0i is S/c\vv S/cS/c, giving field momentum density g=ϵ0E×B\vv g=\epsilon_{0}\vv E\times\vv Bg=ϵ0​E×B.

And two long-standing debts, both settled by name. Chapter 2.1 posed a contradiction between Maxwell and Galileo and offered a fork; the resolution is that Maxwell's equations single out a speed, which lives in the metric, and never singled out a frame — so branch (A) was not merely unsupported by Michelson and Morley, it was structurally impossible. Chapter 1.1 showed Newton's third law failing for two moving charges by −μ0q1q2v2y^/4πd2-\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v^{2}\hat{\vv y}/4\pi d^{2}−μ0​q1​q2​v2y^​/4πd2 and wrote an IOU; §10 found the missing momentum sitting in the field at μ0q1q2v(2x^+y^)/8πd\mu_{0}q_{1}q_{2}v(2\hat{\vv x}+\hat{\vv y})/8\pi dμ0​q1​q2​v(2x^+y^​)/8πd, showed its rate of change cancels the mechanical one exactly — in both components, including a 32\tfrac3223​ that 1.1 never saw — and thereby forced you to accept that a field is not a bookkeeping device but a physical system.

And the thesis, which is the reason the chapter exists. Electromagnetism did not need to be made compatible with relativity. It was relativistic before the word existed, which is exactly why it produced a frame-independent ccc and broke the physics of 1900. What needed fixing was mechanics, and Chapters 2.2 to 2.5 fixed it. The magnetic field is not a second force alongside the electric one; it is what an electric field looks like from a moving frame — an effect of relative order u vd/c2u\,v_{d}/c^{2}uvd​/c2, which for two ordinary currents in copper is about 10−2610^{-26}10−26, and which is visible at all only because the positive and negative charge in matter cancel to at least that precision. A discrepancy in the twenty-sixth significant figure, and it defines a base unit of the SI. Two fields, one tensor; four equations, two lines; and a ccc that belongs to spacetime rather than to any medium. That is the whole of Part II in one chapter, and it is the last thing you need before geometry starts to move.

Where this gets spent.

  • TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν → Chapter 3.6: it is what sits on the right-hand side of the Einstein field equations. Energy gravitates, and now you know what "energy" means as a tensor and why it had to be symmetric.
  • F=dAF=\dd AF=dA and ∂[λFμν]=0\partial_{[\lambda}F_{\mu\nu]}=0∂[λ​Fμν]​=0 → Chapter 3.5, where they become F=dAF=\dd AF=dA and dF=0\dd F=0dF=0 literally, and d2=0\dd^{2}=0d2=0 stops being an analogy.
  • L=−14μ0F2−j ⁣⋅ ⁣A\mathcal{L}=-\tfrac{1}{4\mu_{0}}F^{2}-j\!\cdot\!AL=−4μ0​1​F2−j⋅A → Chapter 5.2, quantised, where the field's normal modes become photons; Chapter 5.8, where −jμAμ-j_{\mu}A^{\mu}−jμ​Aμ becomes the single vertex of QED and every Feynman diagram in the theory is built from copies of it.
  • Gauge freedom → Chapter 6.3, promoted from a convenience to the generating principle: demand it locally and this entire chapter is the output rather than the input. Then Chapter 6.4 repeats the construction with a non-commuting group and gets Yang–Mills, using §9's Lagrangian unchanged except for a commutator.
  • Charge invariance and the E\vv EE–B\vv BB mixing → Chapter 5.5, where the Dirac field's coupling to AμA^{\mu}Aμ is fixed by exactly these transformation properties.
  • The whole structure → Chapter 7.5, where the gauge fields of the Standard Model appear as excitations of an open string, and Chapter 7.7, where FμνFμνF_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}Fμν​Fμν turns out to be the leading term of an expansion on a D-brane whose higher terms are the Born–Infeld action.
